questions.prompt: Which statement about the C++23 definition of `borrowed_range` is correct?

questions.explanation: The concept is `range<R> && (is_lvalue_reference_v<R> || enable_borrowed_range<remove_cvref_t<R>>)`. An lvalue reference is always borrowed, because an algorithm receiving one is not responsible for the object's lifetime. A non-reference `vector<int>`, the case of an rvalue argument, is borrowed only if `enable_borrowed_range` says so, and it does not. Views are not required: `subrange` and `span` are views, but the concept applies to any range.

questions.prompt: In C++23, which temporaries created while evaluating the initializer of a range-based `for` have their lifetime extended to the end of the loop?
options: Only the temporary bound directly to the hidden `__range` reference, as in C++11
Only temporaries of class type with a non-trivial destructor
Every temporary that would otherwise be destroyed at the end of the for-range-initializer full-expression
None: the initializer must not create temporaries other than the range itself
questions.explanation: P2718 added a context to [class.temporary]: a temporary created in the for-range-initializer that would be destroyed at the end of that full-expression instead persists for the lifetime of the `__range` reference, which is the whole loop. Before C++23, only the temporary bound directly to the reference was extended, which is the first option. The rule covers all such temporaries regardless of type, but only in range-based `for`, not in other declarations.
